title: 2024 HMMT Invitational Problem 4
statement:
Given a positive integer \(n\), let \([n]=\{1,2, \ldots, n\}\).

- Let \(a_{n}\) denote the number of functions \(f:[n] \rightarrow[n]\) such that \(f(f(i)) \geq i\) for all \(i\).
- Let \(b_{n}\) denote the number of ordered set partitions of [ \(n\) ], i.e., the number of ways to pick an integer \(k\) and an ordered \(k\)-tuple of pairwise disjoint nonempty sets \(\left(A_{1}, \ldots, A_{k}\right)\) whose union is [ \(n\) ].

Prove that \(a_{n}=b_{n}\).

solutions.text:
Solution: It suffices to define a bijection between the two types of objects in the problem for each \(n\). We'll be a bit more general and define a recursive bijection from ordered set partitions of \(S \subseteq[n]\) to functions \(f: S \rightarrow S\) described in the problem as follows:

If \(S\) is empty, return the trivial function \(f: \varnothing \rightarrow \varnothing\).
Otherwise, consider some ordered set partition \(A_{1}, \ldots, A_{k}\) of \(S \subseteq[n]\), and take \(A_{1}\). Order the elements of \(S\) as \(s_{1}<s_{2}<\cdots<s_{\ell}\). Now, let \(s_{m}\) denote the largest element of \(A_{1}\). Set \(f\left(s_{1}\right)=s_{m}\), and for each \(s_{i} \in A_{1} \backslash\left\{s_{m}\right\}\), set \(f\left(s_{i+1}\right)=s_{1}\).
Then, let \(A_{1}^{\prime}=\left\{s_{i+1}: s_{i} \in A_{1}, s_{i} \neq s_{m}\right\} \cup\left\{s_{1}\right\}\) to be the elements of \(A_{1} \backslash\left\{s_{m}\right\}\) shifted over by 1 index with \(s_{1}\) added in. Create a new ordered set partition of \(S \backslash A_{1}^{\prime}\) by taking the relative ordering of entries of \(A_{2}, \ldots A_{k}\), and relabelling them to match the elements of \(S \backslash A_{1}^{\prime}\). To verify that this reordering can be done, we need to check that the sizes \(\left|A_{1}^{\prime}\right|=\left|A_{1}\right|\). However, \(\left|\left\{s_{i+1}: s_{i} \in A_{1}, s_{i} \neq s_{m}\right\}\right|=\left|A_{1}\right|-1\), and \(s_{1}\) is not in this set, so the new partition is valid.
Let \(f^{\prime}: S \backslash A_{1}^{\prime} \rightarrow S \backslash A_{1}^{\prime}\) be the output of this process recursively applied on the set \(S \backslash A_{1}^{\prime}\) with the new set partition. We can then naturally merge our values of \(f, f^{\prime}\) such that if \(x \in A_{1}^{\prime}, f(x)\) is defined as above, and if \(x \in S \backslash A_{1}^{\prime}\), we take \(f(x):=f^{\prime}(x)\).

We now need to show that this process is well-defined, i.e. any input partition causes it to output a function \(f: S \rightarrow S\) satisfying the desired property, and that it has a well-defined inverse.
First, we observe that the process always outputs a valid function. We can do this by induction; it is vacuously true on the base case \(S=\varnothing\). Then, it suffices to show that if the recursive step output \(f^{\prime}: S \backslash A_{1}^{\prime} \rightarrow S \backslash A_{1}^{\prime}\) satisfies \(f^{\prime}\left(f^{\prime}(i)\right) \geq i\), then adding on the new values of \(f\) for \(A_{1}^{\prime}\) preserves this property. Indeed, we only need to verify it at inputs in \(A_{1}^{\prime}\), which are \(s_{i+1}\) for \(s_{i} \in A_{1}\) with \(i<m\), and also \(s_{1}\).
To check this, let \(s_{i} \in A_{1}\) with \(s_{i}<s_{m}\). Then

\[f\left(f\left(s_{i+1}\right)\right)=f\left(s_{1}\right)=s_{m} \geq s_{i+1}\]

Similarly, it is always true that \(f\left(f\left(s_{1}\right)\right) \geq s_{1}\) since it is the smallest element of \(S\). So, the induction is complete.
Finally, we need to show that this process is invertible. We do this with another recursive process; start any function \(f: S \rightarrow S\) satisfying the desired property. We can then define \(A_{1}\) to be \(\left\{s_{i-1}\right.\) : \(\left.s_{i} \in f^{-1}\left(s_{1}\right), s_{i}>s_{1}\right\} \cup\left\{f\left(s_{1}\right)\right\}\) for \(f^{-1}\left(s_{1}\right)\) the preimage of \(s_{1}\) in \(f\). Note that for any \(s_{i} \in S\) with \(s_{i}>s_{1}\), we do not have \(f\left(s_{i}\right) \in f^{-1}\left(s_{1}\right)\) as otherwise \(f\left(f\left(s_{i}\right)\right)=s_{1}<s_{i}\). Furthermore, no elements of \(S \backslash f^{-1}\left(s_{1}\right)\) can map to \(s_{1}\) due to the definition of a preimage. So, we can restrict \(f\) to a function \(f^{\prime}: S \backslash\left(f^{-1}\left(s_{1}\right) \cup\left\{s_{1}\right\}\right) \rightarrow S \backslash\left(f^{-1}\left(s_{1}\right) \cup\left\{s_{1}\right\}\right)\), on which we can recurse to obtain a partition \(A_{2}, \ldots, A_{k}\) and relabel to \(S \backslash A_{1}\) to obtain a partition \(A_{1}, \ldots, A_{k}\) of \(S\).
This process is well-defined, and is clearly an inverse, as desired.
Below is an example of the bijection for \(n=8\) with the ordered set partition \(\{3,4,6,7\} \cup\{1,5\} \cup\{2,8\}\) :

Step 1
\(A_{1}=\{3,4,6,7\}\)
\(A_{2}, A_{3}:\{1,5\},\{2,8\}\)
Unused elements: \(\{2,3,6,8\}\)
Relabeled \(A_{2}, A_{3}:\{2,6\},\{3,8\}\)

Step 2

\[A_{2}=\{2,6\}\]

\(A_{3}:\{3,8\}\)
Unused elements: \(\{6,8\}\)
Relabeled \(A_{3}:\{6,8\}\)

Step 3

\[A_{3}=\{6,8\}\]
